title: Call by value
body:
The default in C++. The function gets a **copy** of the argument, so anything it does to its
[[Formal parameter]] is done to the copy and the caller's [[Variable]] is untouched.

```c++
void bump(int n) { n = n + 1; }

int x = 5;
bump(x);
cout << x;      // still 5
```

`n` and `x` are two different memory locations that briefly held the same number. When the
function returns, `n` is gone.

The standard demonstration is `swap()`, which does nothing at all until the parameters become
references:

```c++
void swap(int a, int b)   { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }   // does nothing
void swap(int& a, int& b) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }   // works
```

[[Call by reference]] is the other half: `int&` passes the location instead of the value, so
the function can write back. The consequence is the rule in that note, that a
reference argument has to be a variable and not an expression, because there is no location
to pass for `x + 1`.

When to use which:

| Want | Use |
|---|---|
| Function must not change it | value |
| Function must change it | reference, `int&` |
| Function returns two things | reference, since a [[Function]] returns at most one value |
| Big [[Structure]], must not change it | `const` reference, to skip the copy |

The last row is why `const T&` exists: passing by value copies the whole struct every call,
and for anything large that is wasted work. Passing by `const` reference gets the speed of
reference without the ability to modify.

Watch the exception. An [[Array]] passed to a function is *not* copied; the name decays to a
[[Pointer]], so the function can change the caller's array even though nothing in the
signature says `&`. Structs are copied, arrays are not, and that asymmetry catches everybody
once. See [[Compound type]].
